name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
title: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
answer: Local and air-gapped deployment means running AI models and supporting systems entirely on an organization's own hardware and network, with no connection to external cloud services or the public internet. This approach is used in financial data security, governance, and risk work where data cannot leave a controlled environment because of regulation, contract, or sensitivity. The scope covers model serving, data storage, access controls, logging, and update procedures that must all operate without external calls. It also includes deciding which workloads can be isolated and which require external data or model updates.

sections.body: Local and air-gapped deployment means running AI models and supporting systems entirely on an organization's own hardware and network, with no connection to external cloud services or the public internet. This approach is used in financial data security, governance, and risk work where data cannot leave a controlled environment because of regulation, contract, or sensitivity. The scope covers model serving, data storage, access controls, logging, and update procedures that must all operate without external calls. It also includes deciding which workloads can be isolated and which require external data or model updates.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure runs on on-premises servers, private cloud, or dedicated hardware inside the organization's perimeter. Air-gapped systems often use separate physical networks, manual data transfer through controlled media, and internal container or virtual machine platforms. The setup must provide enough compute for model inference and occasional fine-tuning, plus storage for model weights, vector indexes, and audit logs. Network monitoring and physical access controls are part of the infrastructure because the boundary is the main security control.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Models are packaged and transferred into the isolated environment through a review process, then loaded onto local serving software. Data preparation, prompt or query handling, and output review happen inside the boundary, usually with role-based access and versioned model artifacts. Updates require a deliberate transfer window, with hashes and signatures checked before installation. Testing and validation are done on a mirror environment before production changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights concern is that model licenses must permit local deployment, and any restrictions on use, copying, or modification must be checked before transfer. Risk centers on stale threat intelligence, missed security patches, and the difficulty of detecting data exfiltration when the system is intentionally disconnected. Provenance requires a chain of custody for every model file, dataset, and configuration change, recorded in internal logs because no external audit trail exists. Governance also covers who may approve transfers, who may access outputs, and how long logs and model versions are retained.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local and air-gapped deployment is moving toward smaller, more efficient models that can run on modest hardware, and toward standardized packaging formats that make transfer and verification easier. Organizations are also exploring confidential computing and hardware-based attestation to strengthen isolation without sacrificing updates. The trend is toward periodic, controlled synchronization rather than permanent disconnection, balancing security with the need for current models and compliance data.
